subject: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)

messages.author: 7d396ab46d43b4b3
messages.subject: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
parts:
Dear all,

I want to test a multilevel mediation (particularly, test a number of hypotheses about possible mediators of the effect of social class on Right-Wing Authoritarianism) using largely categorical variables surveyed in the General Social Survey, and for this, I would have liked to use Structural Equation Modeling. However, I have doubts about its feasibility, due to missing data.

In fact, there is not a single participant with data on all variables I want to include, because the items were each asked in different waves or ballots. For example, I would have one item that was only asked in ballots A and B, a second item that only occured in ballots B and C, and a third in ballots A and C. Because I am dealing with categorical data, I am considering WLSMV in Mplus, which uses pairwise deletion. In theory, I can draw up a covariance matrix, since every variable co-occurs with every other variable in one ballot or another: for each pair of variables (so for each covariance I need), I have at least 900 participants (though out of a total of more than 10.000 participants). Therefore, intuitively, using list-wise deletion does not seem very problematic to me, since most missings should be MCAR (they result from randomization in the administration of certain ballots/modules) - with perhaps the exception of a few variables that were not asked in particular years/waves. However, when I read about this, it is often recommended that list-wise deletion is not justified when you have more than 10% missings (a threshold that I far exceed here).

Is there a method of dealing with missings that allows me to estimate this model, even though each respondent has randomly missing data on around 50% of the variables? Or is it not feasible/advisable to use SEM in my case?

Thank you in advance for any guidance!

messages.author: b6ae83467b372bc6
messages.subject: Re: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
parts:
Hello,

SEM-approach is very well suited for your purpose.
It seems to me that you used a planned missing design. So, multiple imputation would be your friend dealing with this kind of missingness, see Gonzalez & Rutkowski, 2010. In own studies, we use a balanced incomplete matrix booklet design and applied Multiple Imputation via MICE (see https://osf.io/wa6bn; there is a link to the postprint ).
You can try using fitting a model first with pairwise missing (maybe using the PWL-estimator? as outlined here: https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/cat.html) and compare those results with the results of the model with Multiple Imputations, maybe as a kind of sensitivity analysis. But, your sample size is quiet large, so you will have a lot of options experimenting with that.

Hope, that helps.

kindly,
Marcus

messages.author: b6ae83467b372bc6
messages.subject: Re: SEM with 50% missing data (due to distribution of items over various ballots/waves)
parts:
Dear Thomas,


I am not an expert on MI, but what I have read is quite promising. 50% of missingness, especially if it is a planned missing data design (and in your case, you have a very high N), I do not see any problems. Just consider to use an appropriate numer of imputations and iterations. It is more important to analyze (or better, to know) if the data is MCAR, MAR or MNAR and to analyze the missingness patterns - are these pattens random or do they depend upon certain variables?

Maybe you find some additional information here:

https://www.peterlugtig.com/post/planned-missingness/


I would refer you to this manuals and ressources:
- https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/149140/how-much-missing-data-is-too-much-multiple-imputation-mice-r
- https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd - very good explanation for MI with MICE
- http://hsta559s12.pbworks.com/w/file/fetch/52112520/enders.applied
- maybe this helps, too: https://bmcmedresmethodol.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12874-017-0442-1

Also, consider to play around with the methods for handling missingness, such as in Tabachnik & Fidell: chapter 4.1.3.5 write about cross-checking different missingness-methods. Maybe, try FIML with estimator = MLR first, even you have categorical data, this could help you to get a feeling of what the results can look like.


I wish you the best.
Marcus
